AccessionRequest.description:
The lab accepting a doctor's order onto its bench.

`catalogue_item_id` is chosen here rather than at ordering time on purpose:
a doctor writes "CBC" at speed, and the lab is the one that knows which
catalogue entry that is — and can correct a typo without bouncing the order
back to the consulting room.
AccessionRequest.title: AccessionRequest

AccountBoardEntry.description:
One row on the cash counter's board.

Carries who the patient is, not just which id they are. It also carries
`encounter_status`, because that is what tells the cashier whether the
person is standing in front of them or whether this is a bill left behind by
a death, a referral or a patient who walked out — three situations that need
the same money collected in three very different conversations.
AccountBoardEntry.title: AccountBoardEntry

AdhocSend.description:
A message composed by staff, outside any event trigger.

Still goes through the same dispatcher, and therefore through the same
suppression checks. There is deliberately no path that sends a message
without them.
AdhocSend.title: AdhocSend

AdmissionCreate.description:
Admit a patient. Deliberately short.

An admission happens at 2am with a sick patient in a corridor. Everything
that can be captured later is optional, on the same principle as CLAUDE.md
§7b's four-field registration — the encounter and the bed are what matter,
and a form that blocks on `expected_stay_days` is a form somebody works
around.
AdmissionCreate.title: AdmissionCreate

AdmissionRequestCreate.description: Send a seen patient to the admission desk.
AdmissionRequestCreate.title: AdmissionRequestCreate

AdmissionRequestRead.description:
A row on the admission desk, with the patient already named.

Patient identity is attached by the router through `patients.service`, once
for the whole page, for the same reason the queue board does it: a list of
ids is not a worklist.
AdmissionRequestRead.title: AdmissionRequestRead

AdmissionRequestStatus.description:
Where a patient sent to the admission desk has got to.

Two ways out of PENDING and no way back: an admission made in error is
`Admission.cancel`, not a reopened request, and a patient turned away and
later sent again is a second request with its own author and time.
AdmissionRequestStatus.title: AdmissionRequestStatus

AdmissionSummary.description:
The census row — a ward list is long.

Patient identity and the bed are attached by the router, in bulk. Without
them the census is a list of UUIDs, which is not a census: the question a
charge nurse opens it to answer is "who is in my ward and where", and both
halves of that answer live in other tables.
AdmissionSummary.title: AdmissionSummary

AdmitFromRequest.description: `AdmissionCreate` without the visit — the request already names it.
AdmitFromRequest.title: AdmitFromRequest

AvailabilityExceptionCreate.description: Leave, or an extra clinic on a date the weekly rule does not cover.
AvailabilityExceptionCreate.title: AvailabilityExceptionCreate

BedClass.description:
What the patient is paying for, and what the ward can offer.

Drives the room tariff, so it is an enum rather than free text: a rate card
keyed on a string somebody typed is a rate card with three spellings of
"Semi Private" in it.
BedClass.title: BedClass

BedStatus.description:
The bed lifecycle CLAUDE.md §7b asks for, so availability is never wrong.

`CLEANING` is the rung people leave out, and leaving it out is what makes a
bed board lie: the moment a patient is discharged the bed looks free, so
admissions sends someone to it, and they arrive to find it unmade. Modelling
housekeeping as a state the bed passes through means "available" means
available.
BedStatus.title: BedStatus

BoardBed.description: One cell on the bed board.
BoardBed.title: BoardBed

BoardWard.description: A ward and its beds, as the nursing station screen shows them.
BoardWard.title: BoardWard

ChargeAdd.description:
A line added by hand — a dressing, a consumable, an ambulance.

Most charges arrive automatically from the event bus. This is for what the
events cannot see.
ChargeAdd.title: ChargeAdd

ChargeCategory.description:
What kind of act was billed.

Matters beyond reporting: GST treatment differs by category, and so does
who is allowed to waive it.
ChargeCategory.title: ChargeCategory

CompleteConsultationRequest.description:
The doctor's "I am finished" action (CLAUDE.md §6).

Where the visit goes next is decided by what is still open against it, not
by the doctor picking a status — that is the whole point of the state
machine, and it is one fewer decision on the smallest surface in the system.
CompleteConsultationRequest.title: CompleteConsultationRequest

ConsentType.description: DPDP Act 2023 §6 — consent is per purpose, not a single blanket tick.
ConsentType.title: ConsentType

CriticalCallback.description:
Recording the phone call a panic value demands.

"Called the ward" is not a record. NABH wants to know who was told.
CriticalCallback.title: CriticalCallback

CurrentUserRead.description:
`/auth/me` — adds the resolved authorisation context.

The client uses `permissions` to decide which controls to render. It is
never the authorisation decision itself; that is re-checked server-side on
every request.
CurrentUserRead.title: CurrentUserRead

DailyCount.description: One point on a trend line. Zero-filled — see the module docstring.
DailyCount.title: DailyCount

Dashboard.description:
Whatever the caller's permissions allow, in one round trip.

Assembled server-side for the same reason the consultation chart is: a
dashboard that opens in one request rather than five is the difference
between a screen staff leave open and one they close.

Sections the caller may not see are `None`, not omitted — so the frontend
renders a stable layout instead of reflowing based on role.
Dashboard.title: Dashboard

DateWindow.description:
An inclusive local-date range.

Bounded on purpose. An unbounded report is a full table scan somebody
triggers by leaving a filter blank, and CLAUDE.md §11's "never return
unbounded lists" applies to aggregates too — the cost is in the scan, not
the size of the response.
DateWindow.title: DateWindow

DeathRecord.description: CLAUDE.md §6: datetime, certifying doctor, cause — all three, always.
DeathRecord.title: DeathRecord

DiagnosticDiscipline.description:
Which department does the work. Kept coarse on purpose.

The finer split — haematology vs biochemistry, X-ray vs CT — is a free-text
`section` on the catalogue item, because every hospital organises its
benches differently and an enum would need a migration each time.
DiagnosticDiscipline.title: DiagnosticDiscipline

DischargeRequest.description:
End the stay.

`discharge_type` is required and has no default. A default would be
`RECOVERED`, and a system that quietly records a death as a recovery because
somebody did not change a dropdown is worse than one that asks.
DischargeRequest.title: DischargeRequest

DischargeType.description:
How the stay ended. Every one of these is a different form.

The edge cases are first-class here for the same reason CLAUDE.md §6 makes
them first-class on the Encounter: they are not rare, and treating them as
variations of "discharged" loses the reason.
DischargeType.title: DischargeType

DoctorQueue.description:
One doctor's queue, with the counts reception balances by.

The reception board is a row of these rather than the flat list a nurse
works from, because reception's question is different: not "who is next"
but "which clinic is drowning and which is idle". A doctor with nobody
waiting is included on purpose — an empty column is the answer to that
question, not noise.
DoctorQueue.title: DoctorQueue

DoseRead.description:
One slot on the chart, and enough to give it safely.

Patient identity is attached by the router, and it is not a convenience.
`GET /ipd/doses` without an admission filter is the ward's medication round
— its own docstring says "what is due, **on whom**" — and a round that
cannot say whose dose this is, in which bed, is the single worst list in
the hospital to render as identifiers. Checking the patient against the
chart before giving a drug is the check; the screen has to make it
possible.
DoseRead.title: DoseRead

DoseRecord.description:
A nurse saying what happened to one dose.

`reason` is required for everything except `GIVEN`. A blank reason on a
missed antibiotic is precisely the gap an incident review cannot close, so
it is refused at the boundary rather than nagged about later.
DoseRecord.title: DoseRecord

DoseStatus.description:
One slot on the medication chart.

`DUE` is the state a materialised dose starts in. Everything else is a nurse
saying what happened, and three of them are ways of saying "not given" that
a hospital must be able to tell apart: the patient refused, the ward ran out,
or a doctor held it.
DoseStatus.title: DoseStatus

DrugSchedule.description:
Drugs and Cosmetics Rules schedules (CLAUDE.md §9).

H and H1 need a prescription on file; X needs one retained for two years and
a stricter dispensing record. Carried on the order so the pharmacy module can
validate hard rather than by convention.
DrugSchedule.title: DrugSchedule

DuplicateCandidate.description:
A possible existing record, surfaced while reception types.

`reason` is shown verbatim to staff — "same mobile" is far more actionable
than a bare confidence number they have no way to calibrate.

is_exact.description: True only for an identity collision — same normalised name AND same mobile. A high score alone is not this: two different people genuinely share a name on different numbers.
is_exact.title: Is Exact

DuplicateCandidate.title: DuplicateCandidate

EncounterChart.description:
Everything the consultation screen needs, in one round trip.

Assembled server-side deliberately: the doctor's screen opening in one
request rather than six is most of the difference between the §7b 60-second
target and missing it.
EncounterChart.title: EncounterChart

EncounterEventRead.description: One row of the patient timeline (CLAUDE.md §7b).
EncounterEventRead.title: EncounterEventRead

EncounterOpen.description:
Open a visit directly — casualty, or a walk-in with no appointment.

The OPD path does not use this: check-in and quick-OPD open the encounter
automatically, because making reception do it as a second step is exactly
the kind of forgotten click CLAUDE.md §7b exists to remove.
EncounterOpen.title: EncounterOpen

EncounterStatus.description:
The patient journey, exactly as CLAUDE.md §6 defines it.

Order matters only for readability; legality lives in `state_machine.py`.
EncounterStatus.title: EncounterStatus

EncounterSummary.description: The work-list row. Deliberately light — a busy OPD list is long.
EncounterSummary.title: EncounterSummary

FollowUpCompliance.description:
CLAUDE.md §13 step 10: follow-up compliance.

"Advised" counts visits where a doctor set a follow-up date. "Honoured"
counts those where the patient actually came back on or after it.

Pending visits — the date has not arrived yet — are excluded from the rate
rather than counted as failures. Including them would make the number depend
on when the report is run, which is how a compliance metric becomes
something nobody trusts.
FollowUpCompliance.title: FollowUpCompliance

Gender.description:
Includes `OTHER`: the Transgender Persons Act 2019 makes a third option
a legal requirement on Indian health records, not a nicety.
Gender.title: Gender

code.description: Short uppercase tenant code, e.g. 'KMC'. Cannot be changed later.
code.title: Code

HospitalUpdate.description:
Every field optional — `code` is deliberately absent.

The code is printed on patient cards and embedded in identifiers; letting
it change would orphan records that are already on paper.
HospitalUpdate.title: HospitalUpdate

InpatientReport.description: CLAUDE.md §13 step 10: ALOS, plus how stays ended.
InpatientReport.title: InpatientReport

InvoiceDraftRequest.description:
Assemble every pending charge on a visit into a draft.

`rate_card_id` is optional: left out, the hospital's default card applies,
which is what a walk-in cash patient gets.
InvoiceDraftRequest.title: InvoiceDraftRequest

InvoiceIssueRequest.description: Issuing freezes the lines. Nothing here can change them.
InvoiceIssueRequest.title: InvoiceIssueRequest

InvoiceSummary.description: The worklist row — a busy counter's screen is long.
InvoiceSummary.title: InvoiceSummary

LamaRecord.description:
Left against medical advice, or absconded.

`lama_form_signed` is recorded either way: an unsigned LAMA is the
hospital's legal exposure, and pretending otherwise helps nobody.
LamaRecord.title: LamaRecord

NarrativeEntry.description: A radiologist's report, and the prose half of a pathology one.
NarrativeEntry.title: NarrativeEntry

NoteType.description:
SOAP, plus the two notes staff rather than doctors write.

Split into typed rows instead of one free-text blob so a discharge summary
can be assembled later (`ipd`, Phase 9) without parsing prose, and so a
doctor's template can target one section.
NoteType.title: NoteType

NotificationCategory.description:
What the message is about.

Carried so a patient can opt out of billing reminders without also opting
out of "your biopsy result is ready" — a single global unsubscribe is the
wrong granularity for a hospital.
NotificationCategory.title: NotificationCategory

NotificationChannel.description:
The three ways a message leaves the building (CLAUDE.md §9).

Ordered by preference in configuration, not here — a hospital whose patients
are not on WhatsApp should be able to reorder the ladder without a deploy.
NotificationChannel.title: NotificationChannel

NotificationSummary.description:
The outbox row — the list screen is long.

Carries the patient's name and UHID, not only their id. The outbox exists
to answer "I never got the message", which is a sentence a named person
says at a counter; a page of UUIDs cannot be scanned for them, and the
alternative is a request per row. Attached in bulk by the router.
NotificationSummary.title: NotificationSummary

OccupancyReport.description: CLAUDE.md §13 step 10: occupancy. A snapshot of now, not a range.
OccupancyReport.title: OccupancyReport

OccupancyStats.description: The number management asks for at 9am.
OccupancyStats.title: OccupancyStats

has_more.title: Has More

PatientDetail.description:
Full record for the patient screen.

`alerts` is always present and always first in the payload's intent: the
safety banner must render before anything else on the page (CLAUDE.md §7b).

age_years.description: Age in whole years, derived from birth_date.
age_years.title: Age Years

PatientDetail.title: PatientDetail

PatientRead.description: List/search projection. Deliberately omits identifiers and address.

age_years.description: Age in whole years, derived from birth_date.
age_years.title: Age Years

PatientRead.title: PatientRead

PatientRegister.description:
Rapid registration — the whole form (CLAUDE.md §7b).

Exactly four required fields: name, mobile, approximate age, gender. Nothing
else gates the queue. Address, guardian and insurance are captured later by
whoever has time, and the target is a registration under 30 seconds.
PatientRegister.title: PatientRegister

PatientUpdate.description:
Everything optional. Name and phone are here too, but changing either
re-checks the identity constraint — see `service.update_patient`.
PatientUpdate.title: PatientUpdate

PayerType.description: Who ultimately settles. Drives which rate card applies.
PayerType.title: PayerType

PaymentMethod.description:
UPI first, because in an Indian hospital in 2026 it usually is
(CLAUDE.md §9).
PaymentMethod.title: PaymentMethod

PendingItems.description: Why a visit will not close yet — in words reception can act on.
PendingItems.title: PendingItems

QueueBoardEntry.description:
A queue row with enough about the patient to render a worklist.

`QueueEntryRead` carries identifiers, which is the right shape for the
queue's own logic and the wrong shape for a screen. A doctor's worklist
showing `a3f9c2e1…` instead of a name is not a worklist, and the
alternative — the frontend fetching each patient in turn — is one request
per row on the screen staff refresh most often.

So the router joins the two, once, through `patients.service` rather than
a raw query across the module boundary (CLAUDE.md §2).

The fields are optional because a queue row outlives nothing: a patient
record that has been soft-deleted since check-in leaves the row intact and
the name absent, which is more honest than failing the whole board.

Note this is a *staff* view. A public waiting-room display showing token
numbers only is a different endpoint, unauthenticated, and deliberately
not this one — patient names must not be on a screen the waiting area can
read.
QueueBoardEntry.title: QueueBoardEntry

QueuePriority.description:
Lower sorts first. Values are spaced so a new tier can be slotted between
two existing ones without renumbering rows that are already printed on
tokens.
QueuePriority.title: QueuePriority

QueueReassignRequest.description: Move a waiting patient to another doctor's queue.
QueueReassignRequest.title: QueueReassignRequest

QueueReorderRequest.description:
Put a token right after another one in the same doctor's line.

`None` means the top. A neighbour rather than an index, so the request
still means what the receptionist meant if a walk-in joined while they
were dragging.
QueueReorderRequest.title: QueueReorderRequest

QueueSnapshot.description: Live queue analytics. A snapshot of the current local day.
QueueSnapshot.title: QueueSnapshot

QueueSummary.description: The live queue board for one doctor.
QueueSummary.title: QueueSummary

QuickOpdRequest.description:
One-click OPD (CLAUDE.md §7b).

Reception picks a patient and a doctor; the appointment, the check-in and
the token all happen in this single call. The alternative — book, then find
the booking, then check in, then issue a token — is four screens for the
single most repeated action of the day.
QuickOpdRequest.title: QuickOpdRequest

QuickOpdResponse.description:
Everything the token slip needs, in one response.

Including who the patient is. The slip carried a token number, a doctor and
a room and nothing that identified the person holding it — so the piece of
paper a patient walks away with could not be matched back to their record,
by them or by anybody else. `uhid` is also what the QR on the slip encodes
(CLAUDE.md §7b), which makes this the field the whole scanned-card feature
is printed from.
QuickOpdResponse.title: QuickOpdResponse

RecipientType.description:
Who the message is addressed to — not who it is *about*.

The distinction carries the whole deceased rule. A message **about** a
deceased patient addressed to **staff** ("this bill still needs settling
with the family") is legitimate and necessary; CLAUDE.md §6 requires the
settlement flow to run. The same fact addressed to the patient's own mobile
is the thing that must never happen. Suppression keys on
`recipient_type = PATIENT`, so both stay true at once.
RecipientType.title: RecipientType

ReferenceRangeCreate.description:
A normal band for one kind of patient.

Leave `sex` and the age bounds null for the catch-all band; the service
picks the most specific match and falls back to it.
ReferenceRangeCreate.title: ReferenceRangeCreate

RegistrationResponse.description: The new patient plus any near-duplicates worth a second look.

age_years.description: Age in whole years, derived from birth_date.
age_years.title: Age Years

RegistrationResponse.title: RegistrationResponse

ReportSummary.description: The worklist row — the lab's screen is long.
ReportSummary.title: ReportSummary

ResultEntry.description:
One measured value.

Identified by `analyte_code` rather than id: a technician typing from a
machine printout works in codes, and the codes are stable while ids are not
anything a human ever sees.
ResultEntry.title: ResultEntry

ResultsSubmission.description: A batch of values. Entering a CBC is one action, not twelve.
ResultsSubmission.title: ResultsSubmission

RevenueReport.description:
CLAUDE.md §13 step 10: revenue.

Three different numbers that are easy to confuse and expensive to confuse:
what was *earned* (charges raised), what was *collected* (cash in), and what
is *outstanding* (issued and unpaid). They are reported separately and never
summed.
RevenueReport.title: RevenueReport

role_codes.description: The user's complete role set after this call.
role_codes.title: Role Codes

SafetyBanner.description:
The persistent patient-safety header (CLAUDE.md §7b).

Carried on the chart response rather than fetched separately, because a
banner that arrives one request later than the screen is a banner that gets
missed at exactly the wrong moment.
SafetyBanner.title: SafetyBanner

SearchHit.description:
One result, already phrased for a screen.

`title` and `subtitle` are composed on the server rather than assembled by
the client from six nullable ids. Five kinds of hit render in one list, and
a client formatting each of them differently is five chances to disagree
about how a patient is named.

The ids are all here because the *destination* is the client's business —
the backend has no idea what a route looks like and must not learn.
SearchHit.title: SearchHit

SearchHitKind.description: What the search matched, so the client can route and label the hit.
SearchHitKind.title: SearchHitKind

SearchResults.description:
Hits in the order they should be shown — best guess first.

Not paginated, and that is deliberate. This is a lookup box, not a report:
a receptionist who gets thirty results has mistyped, and the fix is to type
more, not to page through. Anything that genuinely needs browsing goes to
the patient index instead.
SearchResults.title: SearchResults

SlotRead.description: A bookable window, derived on demand rather than stored.
SlotRead.title: SlotRead

SummaryUpdate.description: Every section is optional: the doctor edits what is wrong, not everything.
SummaryUpdate.title: SummaryUpdate

SuppressionCreate.description:
Record a block. `DECEASED` is not accepted here.

A death is recorded in `clinical`, and the suppression follows from it
inside that same transaction. Allowing it to be typed in directly would
create a second, editable source of truth for the one rule CLAUDE.md §14
says to guard actively.
SuppressionCreate.title: SuppressionCreate

SuppressionRead.description:
A block on messaging one patient.

The endpoint's own summary is "who is blocked from messaging", and a
`patient_id` does not answer *who*. Name and UHID are attached in bulk by
the router, like every other worklist in the system.
SuppressionRead.title: SuppressionRead

TemplatePreview.description:
Render a template against sample values without sending anything.

Exists because the alternative way to find out that a template has a typo in
a placeholder name is to read it on a patient's phone.
TemplatePreview.title: TemplatePreview

missing.description: Placeholders the template asks for that the context did not supply.
missing.title: Missing

TemplateType.description:
Reusable text a doctor drops into a note (CLAUDE.md §7b).

Central to the low-doctor-effort goal: the fastest clinical note is one
already written.
TemplateType.title: TemplateType

must_change_password.description: When true the client must send the user to a password change screen.
must_change_password.title: Must Change Password

role_codes.description: System or hospital role codes to assign.
role_codes.title: Role Codes

VisitAccount.description:
Everything the cash counter needs about one visit, in one response.

Assembled server-side for the same reason as the doctor's chart: a screen
that opens in one request rather than four is most of the difference between
hitting the §7b speed targets and missing them.
VisitAccount.title: VisitAccount

VitalsCreate.description:
Every field optional: a nurse records what they actually measured.

Demanding a complete set would only teach staff to type zeros, and a
fabricated respiratory rate is worse than a missing one.
VitalsCreate.title: VitalsCreate

Weekday.description:
Matches `datetime.date.weekday()` — Monday is 0.

An IntEnum rather than a string so comparisons against Python's own weekday
arithmetic need no translation table, which is exactly the kind of mapping
that eventually gets one day out.
Weekday.title: Weekday

WorklistEntry.description:
One open request, with everything needed to work it and to be sure who
it belongs to.

Patient identity is on the row rather than a `patient_id` for the client to
resolve. A worklist of UUIDs is not a worklist, and a technician who has to
open each row to find out whose blood this is will batch them — which is how
a STAT troponin ends up processed fourth.
WorklistEntry.title: WorklistEntry

WorklistStage.description:
What one diagnostic request is waiting for.

get.description:
The cash counter's board: every visit that still owes something, oldest
debt first.

Two bulk lookups decorate the page — the visits through `clinical.service`,
the patients through `patients.service` — so the cost is flat in the number
of rows rather than three queries per row.
Everything the cash counter needs about one visit, in one round trip.

`needs_pricing=true` is the exception worklist: care that was delivered
and that nobody has been able to put a price on.

post.description:
For what the event bus cannot see — a dressing, a consumable, an
ambulance. Everything else is captured automatically.

The care stays on the clinical record; the money does not. Audited with
the amount, because this is the lever somebody would pull to make money
disappear.

patch.description:
Settling a claim records the insurer's money against the invoice — from

get.description:
`awaiting_settlement=true` is the bills left behind by a death, a referral
or a patient who walked out (CLAUDE.md §6).

post.description:
Gathers every pending charge on the visit. Re-runnable: called again
after a later charge lands, it pulls the new line onto the same draft
rather than opening a second one.

Releases the charges back onto the running bill — the care still happened
and still belongs on whatever invoice replaces this one.

One-way door: after this the lines are frozen and the patient has a
printout. A correction is a credit note, not an edit.

UPI first (CLAUDE.md §9). Clearing the last balance closes the visit by
itself, exactly as verifying the last lab report does.

Bad debt. Terminal, and it releases the visit's closure gate — which is
how an absconded patient's encounter stops sitting open forever.

get.description: With `method` and `since`, this is the shift's collection report.

post.description:
Writes a second, reversed row. The original receipt stays exactly as it
was printed, because the cash drawer reconciles against what happened.

One card per payer: cash, an insurer's negotiated list, a scheme's
package rates (CLAUDE.md §9).

The card a walk-in cash patient gets, and the fallback for everyone whose
scheme has no card configured. Exactly one per hospital.

`code` is what links this to the rest of the system: a diagnostics
catalogue entry or a clinical order with the same code prices against it.

Returns the *replacement*. The original survives as `AMENDED` — somebody

Cancels the clinical order too, so an abandoned study stops holding the

NABH wants the call documented: who was told, and when.

Visible to clinicians, clearly provisional, and it does not close the
visit — a provisional number is something to look at, not to act on.

Values are flagged against the reference band that fits this patient's
sex and age, and the band used is copied onto each result.

Signing off clears the clinical order — and if it was the last item
outstanding, the visit closes itself (CLAUDE.md §6).

post.description:
The order stays open: the test was still asked for and still has to

get.description:
Every open lab and radiology request, in the order the bench should work
them, each carrying the one thing it is waiting for.

Built from *orders*, not reports. A request that nobody has accessioned yet
has no report to list, and it is exactly the one most likely to be
forgotten — a worklist assembled from reports only ever shows work somebody
already remembered to start.

Three bulk lookups decorate the whole page — reports, samples, patients —
rather than three per row. The cost is flat in the length of the list, which
is what stops the busiest screen in the building from being the slowest.

post.description:
The key rule of CLAUDE.md §6.

Whether this closes the visit or parks it in `AWAITING_RESULTS` /
`PENDING_CLEARANCE` depends on what is still open against it — the doctor
does not choose, and the patient does not have to walk back to reception.

Terminal, audited, and it flags the patient record in the same transaction.

That last part is what stops a follow-up SMS ever reaching the family
(CLAUDE.md §14).

The clinical signature — and the one place a role check backs the permission.

A signature carries a registration number and clinical responsibility. An
administrator who holds `summary:sign` for operational reasons is not a
clinician, so the role is checked as well.

get.description:
Every ward, every bed, who is in it — in one round trip.

Not paginated, deliberately, and the one place in the system that is exempt
from CLAUDE.md §11's rule. The response is bounded by the hospital's
physical bed count, which is a number in the hundreds that changes when
somebody builds a wing. A paginated bed board is a bed board nobody can see
at a glance, which defeats its only purpose.

post.description:
Compose and send from the counter.

Goes through the same dispatcher as every triggered message, so the same
suppression checks apply. There is deliberately no route that sends without
them.

Record a block a patient asked for, or a number that bounces.

A death is not recordable here — it is written by the clinical death entry,
inside that transaction. See `service.suppress`.

Release a block. A death suppression is refused, whatever the caller holds.

The refusal is in the service, not in RBAC: permissions are data-driven rows
an administrator can edit (CLAUDE.md §8), and this is the one rule that must
not be grantable.

get.description:
Open the record a card names (CLAUDE.md §7b: QR-based patient lookup).

Declared **above** `/{patient_id}`: FastAPI matches in order, and a literal
segment registered after a `uuid.UUID` parameter would never be reached —
`by-uhid` would be parsed as a malformed UUID and 422 instead.

Exact match, not the search box's substring one, and it follows a merge so
a card printed before two records were joined still opens the surviving
one, allergies included.

Audited separately from `patient.view` because a scan is a distinct access
pattern: an auditor asking "who looked this patient up, and how" gets a
different answer for a card presented at a counter than for a click on a
worklist. The scanned value is recorded even when nothing is found — an
unrecognised card is exactly the event somebody investigates later.
get.summary: Resolve one UHID — the scanned-card lookup

get.description:
Reception's view (CLAUDE.md §7b, role-based dashboards).

Every active doctor appears, with or without patients — the empty column
is the one reception is looking for when a clinic is running behind and
they need somewhere to send the next walk-in. Ordered busiest first, so
the problem is at the top and the relief is at the bottom.

Built from two bounded reads (all doctors, all of today's tokens) and one
identity join, so it costs the same whether ten people are waiting or two
hundred.

post.description:
Reception's load-balancing action.

Three records name the doctor — the token, the booking and the chart — and
all three move in one transaction. The chart goes through `clinical`'s
service (CLAUDE.md §2), which refuses once the consultation has begun; a
refusal from either module rolls the whole move back, so a rejected move
burns no token number in the new doctor's series.
post.summary: Move a waiting patient to another doctor

post.description:
The drag-and-drop on reception's board (CLAUDE.md §7b).

Changes rank only — never the priority tier, which stays a fact about the
patient (senior citizen, emergency) rather than about where staff chose
to put them today. Audited: jumping somebody up the line is a decision
that has to be answerable afterwards.
post.summary: Change a token's place in its doctor's line

post.description:
The "Seen" button on reception's board.

The token and booking close, and the chart moves out of `REGISTERED`
through `clinical`'s state machine so the night's auto-close does not
file the visit as a no-show. All in one transaction: a patient is either
seen everywhere or nowhere.
post.summary: Reception marks the patient as seen by the doctor

get.description: Everything this user is allowed to see, in one round trip (CLAUDE.md §7b).
`running_late` is §7b's doctor delay alert, ready for reception's screen.
Earned, collected and outstanding — three numbers, deliberately not summed.

kind of thing it is.

Audited like `/patients/search` and for the same reason: under the DPDP Act
a lookup of personal data is an access, whether or not the person opens the
record afterwards. The query is recorded, the results are not.
